지도에 표시한 건물·시설 안내.title_en: Guide to the Buildings and Facilities Shown on the Map
지도에 표시한 건물·시설 안내.body_en: For each building and facility placed on the Hanyang 3D map, this guide gives a brief introduction, the period it existed, and sources. Placement coordinates, model dimensions and how the map was read are in `gis/buildings/1750_landmarks.json` and the respective work logs (devlog).

읽는 법.body_en:
- **Period of existence** is the span during which the building or institution actually existed. It is not the same as the moment the map model represents. The map's reference point is the mid-18th century (around 1750), when the Doseong Daejido (Great Map of the Capital) was drawn. The Seoul City Wall Museum dates the map to 1753–1760, because it bears the name of Yuksanggung (毓祥宮), which was elevated in 1753. ([Seoul City Wall Museum, Doseong Daejido](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/scwm/relic/RelicView.do?mcsjgbnc=PS01003026001&mcseqno1=014165&mcseqno2=00000&cdLanguage=KOR))
- Only dates confirmed in the sources below are given. Values that could not be confirmed are marked **unconfirmed**.
- **Around 1750** notes whether the building existed at the map's reference time and whether the model departs from it in any way.
- All models are simplified conceptual models, not measured reconstructions.

경회루 터.body_en:
An artificial pond on the west side of Gyeongbokgung. It was enlarged in 1412, and the Gyeonghoeru pavilion stood on its eastern island. The pavilion burned during the Imjin War (1592), but its 48 stone pillars remained standing in the pond.

- **Period of existence**: Pond enlarged and pavilion built in 1412. Pavilion destroyed by fire in 1592. Rebuilt in 1867. The pond survives today.
- **Around 1750**: Only the pond and stone pillars existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido shows a square pond, a row of pillars and two islands inside the wall. Because the actual pond abuts the west wall of Gyeongbokgung, the model was shifted toward the west wall relative to the drawing but kept about 12 m from it, and shown at half size (64 × 57 m) to match the wall, which is drawn narrower than in reality.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Gyeonghoeru](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B2%BD%ED%9A%8C%EB%A3%A8)

근정전 터.body_en:
The site where Geunjeongjeon, the main throne hall of Gyeongbokgung, once stood. In 1750 there was no building; only the two-tier stone terrace (woldae) and foundation stones remained, and the site was used for civil service examinations and the announcement of successful candidates.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1395. Destroyed by fire in 1592. Rebuilt in 1865–1867. Survives today.
- **Around 1750**: **There was no building.** Only the terrace (2.72 m high) and a 5 × 5-bay grid of foundation stones are shown. Since the original map shows no building inside the wall, the position was set from the north–south proportions of Gwanghwamun and the wall.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Geunjeongjeon](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B7%BC%EC%A0%95%EC%A0%84), [Korea Heritage Service: Geunjeongjeon, Gyeongbokgung](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/gungDetail/gogungDetail.do?serial_number=161&detail_code=11&gung_number=1)

사정전·강녕전·교태전 터.title_en: Sajeongjeon, Gangnyeongjeon and Gyotaejeon Sites (Council Hall and Royal Residences)
사정전·강녕전·교태전 터.body_en:
Along the central axis north of Geunjeongjeon stood, in sequence, Sajeongjeon (the king's council hall), Gangnyeongjeon (the king's sleeping quarters) and Gyotaejeon (the queen's sleeping quarters). All burned in 1592, leaving only their sites.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1395. Destroyed by fire in 1592. Rebuilt in 1865–1867. Gangnyeongjeon and Gyotaejeon were moved to Changdeokgung in 1918 and restored in 1995.
- **Around 1750**: **There were no buildings.** Only the platforms and foundation stones are shown. Because the wall on the original map is narrower than in reality, the actual spacing north of Geunjeongjeon was reduced by a factor of about 0.67.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Sajeongjeon](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%AC%EC%A0%95%EC%A0%84), [Wikipedia (Korean): Gangnyeongjeon](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B0%95%EB%85%95%EC%A0%84), [Wikipedia (Korean): Gyotaejeon](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B5%90%ED%83%9C%EC%A0%84)

창덕궁.body_en:
The second palace of Joseon, which long served as the principal palace after Gyeongbokgung burned in the Imjin War. On the map, the area around Injeongjeon, its throne hall, is shown as a hall with a two-tier roof.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1405. Destroyed in the Imjin War in 1592, rebuilt around 1610. Survives today.
- **Around 1750**: In use as the palace where the king resided. Placed where the original map shows the cluster of hall roofs.
- **Sources**: [Korea Heritage Service, Royal Palaces and Tombs Center: Changdeokgung](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R102010000.do)

돈화문.body_en:
The south main gate of Changdeokgung. The original map shows the characters 敦化門 and a gate symbol, so it was placed there.

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1412. Destroyed in the Imjin War, rebuilt around 1609. Survives today.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The model is a two-story gate tower five bays wide (the middle three bays being the gateway). The bay count follows the surviving building; the dimensions are approximate.
- **Guards**: One gate captain (sumunjang, in gugunbok military dress: a felt hat, blue sleeveless coat, red-sleeved jacket and sword) and four Hullyeon Dogam (Military Training Command) soldiers with spears were placed in front of the gate. This follows a record that guard duty outside the Changdeokgung walls was divided among the Hullyeon Dogam at Donhwamun, the Geumwiyeong at Geumhomun and the Eoyeongcheong at Honghwamun; the number of men and the soldiers' dress are not from records but estimates for display. ([Uri Yeoksa Net: Palace wall guard duty](https://contents.history.go.kr/front/nh/print.do?levelId=nh_030_0040_0050_0010_0040), [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Sumunjangcheong](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0031377), [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Gugunbok](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0005662))
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Donhwamun](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0016240)

금호문.body_en:
A gate in the west wall of Changdeokgung. The sectional map shows the characters 金虎門 and a gate symbol on the west wall, so it was placed there facing west.

- **Period of existence**: Named by Seo Geo-jeong in 1475 (6th year of Seongjong). The year of its rebuilding after the Imjin War could not be confirmed. Survives today.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. A simplified model of a single-bay raised gate (sotseul daemun) with a gabled roof.
- **Guards**: One gate captain and two Geumwiyeong soldiers were placed. This follows a record that the Geumwiyeong was responsible for guarding Geumhomun; the number of men is an estimate for display.
- **Sources**: [Korea Heritage Service, Palace Signboards and Couplets – Gates of Changdeokgung](https://www.cha.go.kr/newsBbz/selectNewsBbzView.do?newsItemId=155588792&sectionId=ocp&mn=NS_01_02), [Annals of Seongjong, 6th year, 8th month, 23rd day](https://sillok.history.go.kr/id/kia_10608023_007), [Wikipedia (Korean): Geumhomun, Changdeokgung](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%B0%BD%EB%8D%95%EA%B6%81_%EA%B8%88%ED%98%B8%EB%AC%B8), [Uri Yeoksa Net: Palace wall guard duty](https://contents.history.go.kr/front/nh/print.do?levelId=nh_030_0040_0050_0010_0040)

금위영.body_en:
One of the Five Military Commands, responsible for defending the capital, guarding Changdeokgung and Changgyeonggung, and escorting royal processions. Its headquarters was west of Donhwamun of Changdeokgung, in present-day Unni-dong, Jongno-gu.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1682 (8th year of Sukjong) by merging the Jeongchogun of the Ministry of War with the Hullyeon Byeoldae of the Hullyeon Dogam. Absorbed into the Jangeoyeong in 1881 and abolished in 1895.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The lettering in the yellow boxes west of Donhwamun on the original map is too low in resolution to be read as 禁衛營. Following the literature's description of "some 30 m west of Donhwamun," the position was measured westward from Donhwamun on the original map and kept clear of the road and the gate.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Geumwiyeong](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0007930), [Uri Yeoksa Net: Geumwiyeong 1682–1895](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_o300110&code=kc_age_30), [Wikipedia (Korean): Geumwiyeong](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B8%88%EC%9C%84%EC%98%81), [Jongno-gu Culture and Tourism: Site of the Geumwiyeong West Camp](https://tour.jongno.go.kr/tour/tour/indvdlz/view.do?nttId=26815&viewType=BODY&dongCode=1111014900)

관상감.body_en:
The office in charge of astronomy, geography, the calendar, weather observation and the water clock. Its stone observatory platform (Gwancheondae), used for observing the stars, remains in its original position at 206 Wonseo-dong, Jongno-gu, in front of the Hyundai Gye-dong office building.

- **Period of existence**: The Seoungwan was renamed Gwansanggam in 1466 (12th year of Sejo). Demoted to the Saryeokseo in 1506 and restored under Jungjong. Changed to the Gwansangso in 1894. The Gwancheondae is thought to have been built as a small armillary platform (Sogan-uidae) in 1434 (16th year of Sejong); it was dismantled and restored in place in 1984. Survives today (Treasure).
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The lettering in the square boxes around Gwangbang on the original map could not be read as 觀象監. The position of the surviving Gwancheondae was adjusted to Donhwamun on the original map and kept clear of the road.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Gwansanggam](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B4%80%EC%83%81%EA%B0%90), [Uri Yeoksa Net: Duties and organization of the Gwansanggam](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/nh/view.do?levelId=nh_027_0020_0020_0010_0010), [Wikipedia (Korean): Gwancheondae of the Gwansanggam, Seoul](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%9C%EC%9A%B8_%EA%B4%80%EC%83%81%EA%B0%90_%EA%B4%80%EC%B2%9C%EB%8C%80), [Korea Heritage Portal: Gwancheondae of the Gwansanggam, Seoul](http://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=1121117400000)

동관왕묘.body_en:
A shrine to Guan Yu, the general of Shu Han. Located outside Heunginjimun, it is called Dongmyo (East Shrine) and survives at 84 Nangye-ro 27-gil (Sungin-dong), Jongno-gu.

- **Period of existence**: After the Imjin War, at the request of Ming and with a signboard and construction funds from the Wanli Emperor of Ming, construction began in 1599 and was completed in 1601 (34th year of Seonjo). In 1691 (17th year of Sukjong), King Sukjong performed the rites in person. The rites were discontinued in 1908. Survives today (Treasure).
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The Doseong Daejido labels it 關王廟 outside Heunginjimun. Because the lettering overlaps the road, it was placed 36 m to the south.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Donggwanwangmyo, Seoul](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%9C%EC%9A%B8_%EB%8F%99%EA%B4%80%EC%99%95%EB%AC%98), [Korea Heritage Portal: Donggwanwangmyo, Seoul](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=1121101420000), [Uri Yeoksa Net: Gwanwangmyo and Museongwangmyo](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/km/view.do?levelId=km_007_0060_0010_0030_0010)

평시서.body_en:
The office that supervised the sijeon (licensed shops) merchants. It regulated prices, inspected weights and measures such as rulers, measuring cups and scales, and handled sijeon business licenses and the monopoly right to suppress unlicensed trade (geumnanjeongwon).

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392 as the Gyeongsiseo, renamed Pyeongsiseo in 1466 (12th year of Sejo). First located in Gyeonpyeong-bang of the Central District, later moved to Gyeonghaeng-bang of the Central District. Abolished in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 8 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 平市署 just north of the Unjongga sijeon and south of the Wongaksa pagoda, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Pyeongsiseo](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%ED%8F%89%EC%8B%9C%EC%84%9C(%E5%B9%B3%E5%B8%82%E7%BD%B2)), [Wikipedia (Korean): Pyeongsiseo](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%8F%89%EC%8B%9C%EC%84%9C), [Seoul City Wall Museum, Doseong Daejido](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/scwm/relic/RelicView.do?mcsjgbnc=PS01003026001&mcseqno1=014165&mcseqno2=00000&cdLanguage=KOR)

영희전.body_en:
A portrait hall (jinjeon) that enshrined the portraits of past kings including Taejo, Sejo, Wonjong and Sukjong and held rites for them. It stood in present-day Jeo-dong, Jung-gu, near the former site of Jungbu Police Station.

- **Period of existence**: Began in 1619 (11th year of Gwanghaegun) as the Nambyeoljeon. Rebuilt in 1677, renamed Yeonghuijeon in 1690 (16th year of Sukjong). Rebuilt with five chambers in 1748 (24th year of Yeongjo). Moved to the site of Gyeongmogung in 1899.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The Doseong Daejido draws it as 永禧殿 south of Hundo-bang (薰陶坊), surrounded by trees and a wall. The lettering inside the wall was read on section 11, and the model was placed at the center of the wall drawing on the full original map.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Yeonghuijeon](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0037870), [Seoul Historical Archive, Doseong Daejido section 11](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/archive/archiveNew/NR_archiveView.do?ctgryId=CTGRY780&fileId=dae3d5ce-3616-4256-a8b9-ab636d8d8723&fileSn=1100&type=C&upperNodeId=CTGRY780)

비변사.body_en:
A council body created to deal with frontier military matters, which after the Imjin War became the highest organ of late Joseon government, deciding all affairs of state. Its office stood in front of Donhwamun of Changdeokgung.

- **Period of existence**: Set up as a temporary body in 1510 during the Sampo Waeran (Japanese uprising at the three ports). Made a permanent office in 1555. After the Imjin War it took charge of politics, the economy and diplomacy as well. Abolished in 1865 and absorbed into the State Council (Uijeongbu).
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 備邊司 west of Donhwamun next to the Geumwiyeong, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Bibyeonsa](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%B9%84%EB%B3%80%EC%82%AC), [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Bibyeonsa](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%B9%84%EB%B3%80%EC%82%AC(%E5%82%99%E9%82%8A%E5%8F%B8))

자문감.body_en:
An alternate name for the Seongonggam, the office in charge of repairing and constructing buildings inside and outside the palaces; its office stood outside Geumhomun of Changdeokgung.

- **Period of existence**: Seongonggam established in 1392. The name Jamungam used from the reign of Taejong. Demoted to a junior third-rank office in the Sokdaejeon (Supplement to the Great Code). Continued until the end of Joseon.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 紫門監 west of Geumhomun of Changdeokgung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Jamungam](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%9E%90%EB%AC%B8%EA%B0%90(%E7%B4%AB%E9%96%80%E7%9B%A3))

의빈부.body_en:
The office to which royal sons-in-law (buma), the husbands of the daughters of the king and crown prince, belonged. It stood in Won-dong, west of Changdeokgung.

- **Period of existence**: Bumabu in 1444, renamed Uibinbu in 1466. Changed to the Uibinwon in 1894 and incorporated into the Jongjeongbu.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 儀賓府 outside the west wall of Changdeokgung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Uibinbu](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%9D%98%EB%B9%88%EB%B6%80)

창의궁.body_en:
The house where Yeongjo lived as Prince Yeoning before becoming king. It stood in Uitong-bang opposite Yeongchumun of Gyeongbokgung, and even after his accession Yeongjo called it his jamjeo (residence before accession) and visited it often. It is the area around the lacebark pine of present-day Tongui-dong.

- **Period of existence**: In 1707 Sukjong bought the Inpyeongwi residence and gave it to Prince Yeoning. In 1721 Prince Yeoning became heir apparent and moved into the palace. Hyojangmyo was built inside in 1729 and Uisomyo in 1752. Abolished in 1907 and taken into state ownership.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. As Yeongjo's jamjeo it held Hyojangmyo, and Uisomyo was added in 1752. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 彰義宮 outside the west wall of Gyeongbokgung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Changuigung](https://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%B0%BD%EC%9D%98%EA%B6%81(%E5%BD%B0%E7%BE%A9%E5%AE%AE))

봉상시.body_en:
The office in charge of state sacrificial rites, posthumous titles and the royal ceremonial fields. It stood behind the west side of Yukjo Street (the Six Ministries Street).

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Changed to the Jeonnongsi in 1409 and restored as the Bongsangsi in 1421. Renamed Bongsangsa in 1895, abolished in 1907.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 奉常寺 behind the west side of the Ministry of Works, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Bongsangsi](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%B4%89%EC%83%81%EC%8B%9C)

사역원.body_en:
The office that taught Chinese, Mongolian, Jurchen and Japanese studies and handled interpretation and translation. It stood on the west side of Yukjo Street, west of the present-day Sejong Center for the Performing Arts.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1393. Abolished in the Gabo Reform of 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 司譯院 west of the Ministry of Justice, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Sayeogwon](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%AC%EC%97%AD%EC%9B%90)

의영고.body_en:
A storehouse office under the Ministry of Taxation in charge of goods used in the palace such as oil, honey, beeswax and pepper.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 義盈庫 north of the Sayeogwon, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Uiyeonggo](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%9D%98%EC%98%81%EA%B3%A0)

사복시.body_en:
The office in charge of the king's horses and carriages, harness and stock raising. It is the site of the present-day Jongno-gu Office, facing the Hanseongbu and the Ministry of Taxation on the east side of Yukjo Street across the Junghakcheon stream. The site is also said to be that of Jeong Do-jeon's house (the marker stone is to the southwest of it).

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Changed to the Taeboksi in 1894 and abolished in 1895.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it by its alternate name 太僕寺 east of the Junghakcheon, so it was placed at that lettering. The marker stone for Jeong Do-jeon's house site is to the southwest of it.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Saboksi](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%AC%EB%B3%B5%EC%8B%9C)

장흥고.body_en:
An office under the Ministry of Taxation that procured goods such as mats and oiled paper. It stood in Indal-bang of the Western District, in the area of present-day Naeja-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Subordinate office of the Ministry of Taxation from 1405. Incorporated into the Ministry of the Royal Household in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 長興庫 south of Jeokseon-bang, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Jangheunggo](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%9E%A5%ED%9D%A5%EA%B3%A0(%E9%95%B7%E8%88%88%E5%BA%AB)), [Wikipedia (Korean): Jangheunggo](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%9E%A5%ED%9D%A5%EA%B3%A0)

내수사.body_en:
The office that managed the royal family's rice, cloth, sundry goods and slaves. Formally a state institution, it in practice handled the king's private property. Present-day Naesu-dong takes its name from it.

- **Period of existence**: The Naesuso was reorganized as the Naesusa in 1466. Abolished in 1910.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 4 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 內需司 behind the west side of Yukjo Street, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Naesusa](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%82%B4%EC%88%98%EC%82%AC(%E5%85%A7%E9%9C%80%E5%8F%B8))

대보단.body_en:
An altar built on the west side of the rear garden of Changdeokgung to offer rites to the Wanli Emperor of Ming, who sent troops during the Imjin War. Under Yeongjo it was greatly rebuilt, adding the Hongwu and Chongzhen Emperors of Ming.

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1704 on the former site of the Byeoldaeyeong outside Yogeummun in the rear garden of Changdeokgung. Greatly rebuilt in 1749 in accordance with Ming institutions, adding the Hongwu and Chongzhen Emperors. Abolished in 1884.
- **Around 1750**: Existed, just after the major rebuilding of 1749. Section 2 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 大報壇 northwest of the rear garden of Changdeokgung, so it was placed at that lettering as a low platform.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Daebodan](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%8C%80%EB%B3%B4%EB%8B%A8(%E5%A4%A7%E5%A0%B1%E5%A3%87))

장원서.body_en:
The office that managed the palace gardens, flowering plants and fruit trees and was in charge of fruit offered to the court. It stood at the mouth of Samcheong-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Sangnimwon in 1394. Renamed Jangwonseo in 1466. Abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 2 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 掌苑署 south of Samcheongdongmun, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Jangwonseo](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%9E%A5%EC%9B%90%EC%84%9C(%E6%8E%8C%E8%8B%91%E7%BD%B2))

선혜청 북창.body_en:
The north storehouse of the Seonhyecheong (Office of Benevolent Relief), which stored the Daedong tribute rice. It stood at the mouth of Samcheong-dong.

- **Period of existence**: The Seonhyecheong was established in 1608 with the enforcement of the Daedong Law. The north storehouse was located in Samcheong-dong. The Seonhyecheong was abolished in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 2 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 宣惠倉 north of the mouth of Samcheong-dong, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Seonhyecheong](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%A0%ED%98%9C%EC%B2%AD)

북영.title_en: Bugyeong (North Camp of the Military Training Command)
북영.body_en:
A branch camp of the Hullyeon Dogam (Military Training Command) located outside Hongbungmun north of Changdeokgung, in present-day Wonseo-dong. It was also called Hunguk.

- **Period of existence**: The Hullyeon Dogam was established in 1593. The Bugyeong stood at 1 Wonseo-dong outside Hongbungmun of Changdeokgung and had 235 bays of buildings. The Hullyeon Dogam was abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 2 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 北營 outside the northwest wall of Changdeokgung and south of the Daebodan, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Bugyeong](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0024695), [Wikipedia (Korean): Hullyeon Dogam](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%9B%88%EB%A0%A8%EB%8F%84%EA%B0%90)

동활인서.body_en:
An office that treated and relieved the sick in the capital. The Donghwarinseo (east) was placed outside Dongsomun (Hyehwamun) and the Seohwarinseo (west) outside Seosomun.

- **Period of existence**: Dongseo Daebiwon in 1392. Dongseo Hwarinwon in 1414, renamed Hwarinseo in 1466. Abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 3 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 活人署 outside Hyehwamun, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Hwarinseo](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%ED%99%9C%EC%9D%B8%EC%84%9C(%E6%B4%BB%E4%BA%BA%E7%BD%B2))

탕평비각.body_en:
A pavilion protecting the Tangpyeong Stele, which Yeongjo erected in 1742 at the entrance to Seonggyungwan to make known to the Confucian students his policy of impartiality (tangpyeong).

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1742. Survives today.
- **Around 1750**: Existed; it was in its eighth year. Section 3 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 碑閣 at the entrance to Seonggyungwan with a drawing of a small house, so it was placed there.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Tangpyeongbi](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%83%95%ED%8F%89%EB%B9%84)

어의궁(본궁).body_en:
The residence where Hyojong lived as Prince Bongnim before his accession, called Ha-eouigung (Lower Eouigung). It later became the detached palace where kings and crown princes held their wedding rites, and was also known as Joyangnu. It is present-day Yeonji-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Prince Bongnim (Hyojong) began living there in 1631 after his wedding. Detached palace for royal weddings in late Joseon. In 1907 its property passed to the Bureau of Imperial Household Property by ordinance of the Ministry of the Imperial Household.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 6 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 本宮 in Sunggyo-bang east of Changgyeonggung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Eouigung](https://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%96%B4%EC%9D%98%EA%B6%81(%E6%96%BC%E7%BE%A9%E5%AE%AE)), [Seoul Historical Archive, Doseong Daejido section 6](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/archive/archiveNew/NR_archiveView.do?ctgryId=CTGRY780&fileId=8d0c01f5-d2dc-4b74-a478-2597699c6758&fileSn=1100&type=C&upperNodeId=CTGRY780)

훈국신영.title_en: Hunguk Sinyeong (New Headquarters of the Military Training Command)
훈국신영.body_en:
The Sinyeong (New Camp), headquarters of the Hullyeon Dogam (Military Training Command). It stood outside Heunghwamun of Gyeongdeokgung (Gyeonghuigung), in present-day Sinmunno 1-ga, with 197 bays of buildings. It was responsible for defending the capital and guarding the royal palaces.

- **Period of existence**: The Hullyeon Dogam was established in 1593 and organized into five camps in 1594. The Sinyeong was a 197-bay headquarters outside Heunghwamun. The Hullyeon Dogam was abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 7 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 訓局新營 outside Heunghwamun of Gyeongdeokgung, so it was placed at that lettering. It was previously placed south of the Ministry of Taxation following materials on Yukjo Street from around 1863, but has been moved to the lettering on the original map.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture: Hullyeon Dogam](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0065793), [Wikipedia (Korean): Hullyeon Dogam](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%9B%88%EB%A0%A8%EB%8F%84%EA%B0%90)

비변사(경덕궁 앞).title_en: Bibyeonsa (Border Defense Council, in front of Gyeongdeokgung)
비변사(경덕궁 앞).body_en:
The Bibyeonsa office that stood outside Heunghwamun of Gyeongdeokgung. When Yeongjo resided at Gyeongdeokgung, the Bibyeonsa, which oversaw state affairs, also kept an office near the palace. It is marked on the original map separately from the Bibyeonsa in front of Donhwamun.

- **Period of existence**: The Bibyeonsa became a permanent office in 1555. Abolished in 1865.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 7 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 備邊司 outside Heunghwamun of Gyeongdeokgung, east of the Hunguk Sinyeong, so it was placed at that lettering. The same name also appears in front of Donhwamun.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Bibyeonsa](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%B9%84%EB%B3%80%EC%82%AC), [Seoul Historical Archive, Doseong Daejido section 7](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/archive/archiveNew/NR_archiveView.do?ctgryId=CTGRY780&fileId=edc4aa41-2b9b-48ea-8577-c79aad2c0e7d&fileSn=1100&type=C&upperNodeId=CTGRY780)

선공감.body_en:
An office under the Ministry of Works in charge of civil engineering and building repairs. It also handled construction, the making of coffins and the supply of firewood.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Merged into the Jeongaksa in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 7 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 繕工監 outside the south wall of Gyeongdeokgung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Seongonggam](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%84%A0%EA%B3%B5%EA%B0%90(%E7%B9%95%E5%B7%A5%E7%9B%A3))

명례궁.body_en:
The former house of Grand Prince Wolsan, used by Seonjo as a temporary palace after the Imjin War, and afterward a royal estate (gungga) that raised and managed the royal family's private funds. It is the site of present-day Deoksugung.

- **Period of existence**: Used by Seonjo as a temporary palace in 1593. Given the name Gyeongungung in 1611. First recorded as Myeongnyegung in 1623. Its functions diminished with Gojong's expansion of Gyeongungung in 1897, and it was wound up in 1907.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 7 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 明禮宮 in Myeongnye-bang to the southwest, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Myeongnyegung](https://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%AA%85%EB%A1%80%EA%B6%81(%E6%98%8E%E7%A6%AE%E5%AE%AE))

선혜청 신창.body_en:
The head office and new storehouse of the Seonhyecheong (Office of Benevolent Relief), the largest fiscal office of late Joseon, which managed the tribute rice, cloth and money collected under the Daedong Law. It stood inside Sungnyemun, on the site of present-day Namdaemun Market.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1608 with the enforcement of the Daedong Law. Besides the head office (Sinchang) inside Sungnyemun, it had north, south and separate storehouses. Abolished in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 10 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 宣惠新倉 in Sinchang-dong inside Sungnyemun, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Seonhyecheong](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%A0%ED%98%9C%EC%B2%AD), [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Namdaemun Market](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%82%A8%EB%8C%80%EB%AC%B8%EC%8B%9C%EC%9E%A5(%E5%8D%97%E5%A4%A7%E9%96%80%E5%B8%82%E5%A0%B4))

태평관.body_en:
The lodging for envoys from Ming China. It was badly damaged in the Imjin War and the envoys' lodging moved to Nambyeolgung, but some buildings remained and were used for banquets. It is present-day Seosomun-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Newly built after the move of the capital to Hanyang in 1395. Destroyed in the Imjin War, after which Nambyeolgung became the envoys' lodging. The remaining buildings were used for banquets, and after 1908 the area was converted to official residences.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Since Ming had fallen, it was no longer used as an envoys' lodging, but section 10 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 大平館, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Taepyeonggwan](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%ED%83%9C%ED%8F%89%EA%B4%80(%E5%A4%AA%E5%B9%B3%E9%A4%A8))

예빈시.body_en:
The office in charge of entertaining envoys and providing food for royal relatives and high officials. It was in Yangsaeng-bang of the Western District until it moved inside Nambyeolgung in 1778.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Moved from south of the State Council to Yangsaeng-bang of the Western District, then inside Nambyeolgung in 1778. Abolished in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed, at the time in Yangsaeng-bang. Section 10 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 禮賓寺 east of the Yangsaeng-bang lettering, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Yebinsi](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%98%88%EB%B9%88%EC%8B%9C(%E7%A6%AE%E8%B3%93%E5%AF%BA))

남관왕묘.body_en:
A shrine to Guan Yu, called Nammyo (South Shrine) because it stood outside Sungnyemun. It was the first Guan Yu shrine, built by Ming troops during the Imjin War.

- **Period of existence**: Built outside Sungnyemun in 1598. Burned in 1952 and rebuilt in 1957. Moved to Sadang-dong, Dongjak-gu, in 1979.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 10 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 關王廟 to the south outside Sungnyemun, so it was placed at that lettering. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Nammyo](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%82%A8%EB%AC%98)

어영창.body_en:
The south storehouse (Namchang) of the Eoyeongcheong (Royal Guard Command). It stood north of the Namsoyeong and had 137 bays.

- **Period of existence**: Newly built as the Eoyeongcheong south storehouse in 1692. The Eoyeongcheong was abolished in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 12 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 御營倉 north of the Namsoyeong, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Namchang (Joseon)](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%82%A8%EC%B0%BD_(%EC%A1%B0%EC%84%A0))

남소영.title_en: Namsoyeong (South Camp of the Royal Guard Command)
남소영.body_en:
A branch camp of the Eoyeongcheong (Royal Guard Command) and gunpowder magazine at the foot of Namsan beside Namsomun. Jangchungdan was later built on its site.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1695. Offices of 194 bays and a powder magazine of 52 bays. Abolished around 1895, and Jangchungdan was built on the site in 1900.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 12 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 南小營 at the foot of Mongmyeoksan (Namsan) inside Namsomun, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Namsoyeong](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%82%A8%EC%86%8C%EC%98%81(%E5%8D%97%E5%B0%8F%E7%87%9F))

소현묘.body_en:
A shrine that enshrined the spirit tablets of Crown Prince Sohyeon, eldest son of Injo, and his consort Crown Princess Kang. It stood beside Yuksanggung, and in 1776 the tablets were moved to the tomb and it became Yeonggyeongjeon.

- **Period of existence**: After Crown Prince Sohyeon's death in 1645, he was enshrined together at Sunhoemyo, which was enlarged to four bays. Crown Princess Kang's tablet was enshrined in 1718. In 1776 the tablets were moved to the tomb and the shrine renamed Yeonggyeongjeon.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 1 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 昭顯廟 west of Yuksanggung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Sohyeonmyo](https://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%86%8C%ED%98%84%EB%AC%98(%E6%98%AD%E9%A1%AF%E5%BB%9F)), [Seoul Historical Archive, Doseong Daejido section 1](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/archive/archiveNew/NR_archiveView.do?ctgryId=CTGRY780&fileId=8574fb02-d3c9-4b3b-9098-4393d481c4d6&fileSn=1100&type=C&upperNodeId=CTGRY780)

세검정.body_en:
A pavilion on the rocks of the Hongjecheon stream outside Changuimun. It is said to be where the draft records (sacho) were washed away after the Annals (Sillok) were completed. It burned in 1941 and was rebuilt in 1977.

- **Period of existence**: Thought to have been built around 1500–1505. Rebuilt in 1747 under Yeongjo. Destroyed by fire in 1941, restored in 1977. Seoul Monument.
- **Around 1750**: Existed, just after the rebuilding of 1747. Section 1 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 洗劍亭 by the Hongjecheon outside Changuimun, so it was placed at that lettering as a small pavilion. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Segeomjeong (Seoul)](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%B8%EA%B2%80%EC%A0%95_(%EC%84%9C%EC%9A%B8))

남별궁.body_en:
A royal estate that Seonjo built on the house site of Princess Gyeongjeong, daughter of Taejong, and gave to Prince Uian. After the Imjin War it became the place where Chinese envoys stayed and were entertained. In 1897 the Hwangudan (Altar of Heaven) was built on the site. It is the site of the present-day Chosun Hotel in Sogong-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Built by Seonjo in 1583 with some 200 bays and given to Prince Uian. Envoys' lodging after the Imjin War. From Sukjong's reign the Yeongjeop Dogam (Reception Office) handled the entertainment of envoys. Disappeared with the construction of the Hwangudan in 1897.
- **Around 1750**: Existed, at the time used for entertaining Qing envoys. Section 11 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 南別宮 at the mouth of Sogong-dong, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Nambyeolgung](https://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%82%A8%EB%B3%84%EA%B6%81(%E5%8D%97%E5%88%A5%E5%AE%AE)), [Seoul Historical Archive, Doseong Daejido section 11](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/archive/archiveNew/NR_archiveView.do?ctgryId=CTGRY780&fileId=dae3d5ce-3616-4256-a8b9-ab636d8d8723&fileSn=1100&type=C&upperNodeId=CTGRY780)

동학(동부학당).body_en:
A state secondary Confucian school in the Eastern District of Hanseongbu, one of the Four Schools (sahak). It moved to Changseon-bang in 1438 and after the Imjin War survived in little more than name.

- **Period of existence**: Built between 1422 and 1435. Moved to Changseon-bang in 1438. Existed in name only after the Imjin War. Disappeared with the introduction of modern education at the end of Joseon.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 9 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 東學 north of Changseon-bang, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Donghak](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%8F%99%ED%95%99(%E6%9D%B1%E5%AD%B8))

순청.body_en:
The office in charge of crime and fire prevention in the capital, announcing the hours and night patrols. It was divided into left and right offices in 1465.

- **Period of existence**: Existed from early Joseon. Divided into the Left and Right Suncheong in 1465. Transferred to the Police Bureau (Gyeongmucheong) in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 8 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 巡廳 south of the Left Podocheong and north of Unjongga, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Suncheong](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%88%9C%EC%B2%AD(%E5%B7%A1%E5%BB%B3)), [Seoul Historical Archive, Doseong Daejido section 8](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/archive/archiveNew/NR_archiveView.do?ctgryId=CTGRY780&fileId=fe073a1b-2a35-41c6-98da-3c21d7a4ba20&fileSn=1100&type=C&upperNodeId=CTGRY780)

장악원.body_en:
An office under the Ministry of Rites in charge of the music and dance for state ceremonies such as the Jongmyo rites, the Sajik rites and court banquets.

- **Period of existence**: Established as the Jangakseo in 1457, Jangagwon in 1466. Placed under the Ministry of the Royal Household in 1894, abolished in 1895.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 8 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 掌樂院 west of the Hyeminseo and south of the Cheonggyecheon, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Jangagwon](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%9E%A5%EC%95%85%EC%9B%90(%E6%8E%8C%E6%A8%82%E9%99%A2))

종친부.body_en:
The office that administered the king's relatives, kept the genealogies and portraits of past kings, and handled the clothing of the king and queen. It stood in Gwangwang-bang of the Northern District east of Gyeongbokgung, in the area of the present-day National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul.

- **Period of existence**: The Jaenaejegunso was renamed Jongchinbu in 1430. Abolished in 1895 with the establishment of the Jongjeongbu.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 宗親府 in Gwangwang-bang east of Gyeongbokgung, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Jongchinbu](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%A2%85%EC%B9%9C%EB%B6%80(%E5%AE%97%E8%A6%AA%E5%BA%9C))

사간원.body_en:
A remonstrance office that admonished the king for his faults and impeached officials. Present-day Sagan-dong, Jongno-gu, takes its name from it.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1401 by making the Nangsa of the Munhabu independent. Abolished in the Gabo Reform of 1894.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 司諫院 southwest of the Jongchinbu, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Saganwon](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%82%AC%EA%B0%84%EC%9B%90(%E5%8F%B8%E8%AB%AB%E9%99%A2)), [Wikipedia (Korean): Saganwon](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%AC%EA%B0%84%EC%9B%90)

한성부 북부.body_en:
The office that handled the civil administration of the northern area, one of the five districts of Hanseongbu.

- **Period of existence**: From the establishment of the five districts in early Joseon to the end of the dynasty. The exact years of establishment and abolition could not be confirmed.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 北部 south of the Saganwon, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Five Districts (Hanseongbu)](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%98%A4%EB%B6%80_(%ED%95%9C%EC%84%B1%EB%B6%80))

중학(중부학당).body_en:
One of the four schools (sahak) in Hanseongbu, a state school that taught Confucian students. Present-day Junghak-dong, Jongno-gu, takes its name from it.

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1422. Existed in name only after the Imjin War. Disappeared with the introduction of modern education at the end of Joseon.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 5 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 中學 next to the Junghak-gye lettering in Gwangwang-bang, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Junghak](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%A4%91%ED%95%99(%E4%B8%AD%E5%AD%B8))

전옥서.body_en:
The office that managed prisoners held in jail. It stood in Seorin-bang of the Central District, present-day Seorin-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Abolished in 1894 when the Prison Bureau (Gamokseo) was created.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 8 of the Doseong Daejido labels it 典獄署 southeast of the Uigeumbu and south of Unjongga, with 典獄後洞 beside it, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Jeonokseo](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%A0%84%EC%98%A5%EC%84%9C(%E5%85%B8%E7%8D%84%E7%BD%B2))

수진궁.body_en:
Beginning as the estate of Grand Prince Jean, son of Yejong, it became in late Joseon a memorial estate that held rites for grand princes and princes who died without heirs, princesses who died before marriage, and royal concubines without heirs. It is the area of the present-day Jongno-gu Office in Susong-dong.

- **Period of existence**: A new residence was built in 1544 after the death of Grand Prince Jean. Memorial estate in late Joseon. Its estate office was abolished in 1907, and it continued until 1909.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. On the Doseong Daejido the character 宮 straddles the boundary of sections 5 and 8 together with the name box for 壽進坊, so it was placed there. The full name of the estate could not be read in one piece.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Sujingung](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%88%98%EC%A7%84%EA%B6%81(%E5%A3%BD%E9%80%B2%E5%AE%AE))

기로소.body_en:
An office established to honor senior civil officials over seventy. Kings too entered it when they grew old. It stood in Jingcheong-bang of the Central District, in the area of present-day Jongno 1-ga (the site of the Kyobo Building).

- **Period of existence**: Originated when Taejo entered at age sixty; the name Chisa Giroso was fixed in 1428. Became an independent office in 1765. Abolished in 1909.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. Section 7 of the Doseong Daejido clearly labels it 耆老所 at the upper right, at the southeast corner of Yukjo Street, so it was placed at that lettering.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Giroso](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EA%B8%B0%EB%A1%9C%EC%86%8C(%E8%80%86%E8%80%81%E6%89%80))

사온서.body_en:
The office in charge of the wine and sweet rice drink used in the palace. It stood in Jeokseon-bang of the Western District.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. The date of its abolition is unknown; some estimate it disappeared before the early 17th century.
- **Around 1750**: Uncertain. The encyclopedia estimates abolition before the early 17th century, but section 4 of the Doseong Daejido has the lettering 司醞署 in Jeokseon-bang, so it was placed there. Whether the office still existed or only the old name was recorded could not be confirmed.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Saonseo](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%82%AC%EC%98%A8%EC%84%9C(%E5%8F%B8%E9%86%9E%E7%BD%B2))

경기감영.body_en:
The provincial office where the governor of Gyeonggi Province served. It stood southwest outside Donuimun, in present-day Pyeong-dong, Jongno-gu (the area of the Red Cross Hospital).

- **Period of existence**: Established in Suwon in 1413, soon moved to Gwangju, and around 1460 to Hanseong. Abolished in 1895 under the 23-prefecture system.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The Doseong Daejido labels it 京畿監營 beside the Gyeonggyo bridge (京橋) outside Donuimun, so it was placed at that lettering. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Sources**: [Wikipedia (Korean): Gyeonggi Gamyeong](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B2%BD%EA%B8%B0%EA%B0%90%EC%98%81)

모화관.body_en:
The place where Chinese envoys were welcomed and sent off. It stood northwest outside Donuimun, in present-day Hyeonjeo-dong, Seodaemun-gu (the area of Independence Gate).

- **Period of existence**: Built as the Mohwaru in 1407, renamed Mohwagwan in 1430. After Independence Gate was built in 1896, it was converted into Independence Hall in 1897.
- **Around 1750**: Existed. The Doseong Daejido shows a square box that appears to read 慕華館 by the road northwest outside Donuimun, so it was placed there. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Sources**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty: Mohwagwan](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%AA%A8%ED%99%94%EA%B4%80(%E6%85%95%E8%8F%AF%E9%A4%A8))

영은문.body_en:
The gate erected in front of Mohwagwan (the guesthouse for Chinese envoys) to receive envoys from China. It was demolished in 1896, Dongnimmun (Independence Gate) was built just behind its site, and two foundation stones remain.

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1537 as Yeongjomun and renamed Yeongeunmun in 1538. Demolished around the founding of the Korean Empire. The foundation stones were designated a Historic Site in 1963.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. On the Doseongdaejido (Great Map of the Capital), a square box that appears to read 迎恩門 sits by the road south of Mohwagwan, so a small gate marker was placed there. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Mohwagwan](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%AA%A8%ED%99%94%EA%B4%80(%E6%85%95%E8%8F%AF%E9%A4%A8))

전의감.body_en:
The office in charge of medicinal materials used by the royal household and the medicines granted to officials. It also handled medical education and the medical examinations.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392, succeeding the Goryeo Jeonuisi. Abolished in the Gabo Reforms of 1894.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 典醫監 in Gyeonpyeongbang at the bottom of detail sheet 5 of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Jeonuigam](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%A0%84%EC%9D%98%EA%B0%90(%E5%85%B8%E9%86%AB%E7%9B%A3))

충훈부.body_en:
The office that managed and honored merit subjects and their descendants. Early in the reign of Jungjong it moved to Gwaninbang in the Central District, the area of today's Insa-dong and Gwanhun-dong.

- **Period of existence**: Gongsindogam in 1392, Chunghunsa in 1434, Chunghunbu in 1454. In 1894 it became the Gigongguk and was merged into the State Council (Uijeongbu).
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 忠勳府 north of Gwaninbang on detail sheet 5 of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Chunghunbu](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%B6%A9%ED%9B%88%EB%B6%80(%E5%BF%A0%E5%8B%B3%E5%BA%9C))

한성부 중부.body_en:
The office that handled residents' administration for the central area of the capital, one of the five districts of Hanseongbu (the capital magistracy). The marker stone for the office site stands at Sewoon Plaza in front of Jongmyo.

- **Period of existence**: From the establishment of the five districts in early Joseon until the end of the dynasty. Exact years of establishment and abolition were not confirmed.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 中部 south of the east end of Unjongga on detail sheet 8 of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription.
- **Source**: [Seoul&, "The equivalent of today's Jongno-gu Office... the Hanseong magistrate even attended royal councils" (2018)](https://www.seouland.com/arti/culture/culture_general/3813.html), [Korean Wikipedia, Obu (Hanseongbu)](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%98%A4%EB%B6%80_(%ED%95%9C%EC%84%B1%EB%B6%80))

한성부 남부.body_en:
The office that handled residents' administration for the southern area, one of the five districts of Hanseongbu (the capital magistracy). The marker stone for the office site stands between exits 7 and 8 of Euljiro 1-ga Station.

- **Period of existence**: From the establishment of the five districts in early Joseon until the end of the dynasty. Exact years of establishment and abolition were not confirmed.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 南部 by the road south of Cheonggyecheon at the lower left of detail sheet 8 of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription.
- **Source**: [Seoul&, "The equivalent of today's Jongno-gu Office... the Hanseong magistrate even attended royal councils" (2018)](https://www.seouland.com/arti/culture/culture_general/3813.html), [Korean Wikipedia, Obu (Hanseongbu)](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%98%A4%EB%B6%80_(%ED%95%9C%EC%84%B1%EB%B6%80))

사재감.title_en: Sajaegam (Bureau of Fish, Meat and Fuel)
사재감.body_en:
An office under the Ministry of Taxation (Hojo) in charge of the fish, meat, firewood and the like used in the palace. It was in Uitongbang in the Northern District and later moved to Sunhwabang.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392. Abolished in the government reorganization of 1882.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 司宰監 between Sunhwabang and Uitongbang west of Gyeongbokgung on detail sheet 4 of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Sajaegam](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EC%82%AC%EC%9E%AC%EA%B0%90(%E5%8F%B8%E5%AE%B0%E7%9B%A3))

내자시.body_en:
An office under the Ministry of Taxation (Hojo) that supplied the royal household with rice, flour, liquor, soy sauce and banquet provisions. It stood in Indalbang in the Western District; today's Naeja-dong takes its name from it.

- **Period of existence**: Naebusi renamed Naejasi in 1401. Abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 內資寺 west of Jeokseonbang on detail sheet 4 of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Naejasi](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EB%82%B4%EC%9E%90%EC%8B%9C(%E5%85%A7%E8%B3%87%E5%AF%BA))

만리창.body_en:
A granary of the Seonhyecheong (Agency for Tribute Relief). It stood in the pine grove in front of Hyochangwon, in the area of today's Hyochang Park. Japanese troops camped here during the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894.

- **Period of existence**: Years of establishment and abolition were not confirmed. Japanese troops camped on the granary site during the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894.
- **Around 1750**: It is taken to have existed. It is written as 萬里倉 toward Yongsan in the southwest of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription. This inscription also serves as the southwest-corner control point for georeferencing. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Source**: [Korean Wikipedia, Hyochang Park](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%9A%A8%EC%B0%BD%EA%B3%B5%EC%9B%90)

군자감 강감.body_en:
The Yongsan riverside granary (ganggam) of the Gunjagam, an office under the Ministry of Taxation (Hojo) in charge of military provisions and other military supplies. After the late 18th century only the riverside granary remained, and it is said to have stored 300,000 seok of grain.

- **Period of existence**: Gunjagam established in 1392; riverside granary established on the Yongsan river in 1413. Abolished in the Gabo Reforms of 1894.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. It is written as 軍資監 toward Yongsan, south of Mallichang in the southwest of the Doseongdaejido, so it was placed at the position of that inscription. It is taken to be the Yongsan riverside granary, not the main bureau inside the city wall. It lies outside the city wall.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, Gunjagam](http://dh.aks.ac.kr/sillokwiki/index.php/%EA%B5%B0%EC%9E%90%EA%B0%90(%E8%BB%8D%E8%B3%87%E7%9B%A3))

창경궁.body_en:
A palace built by Seongjong by enlarging the site of Sugangung to house the dowager queens; it shared a wall with Changdeokgung and together they formed the East Palace (Donggwol). The map shows the area of its main hall, Myeongjeongjeon, as a single-story roofed hall.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1484. Burned during the Imjin War (Japanese invasions), rebuilt around 1616. Turned into the Changgyeongwon amusement park during the Japanese colonial period and restored as a palace in the 1980s. Extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The original map has no palace name, so it was positioned so that the midpoint between Changgyeonggung and Honghwamun matches the modern location.
- **Source**: [Korea Heritage Service, Royal Palaces and Tombs Center, Changgyeonggung](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R103010000.do)

홍화문.body_en:
The main gate of Changgyeonggung, facing east.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1484. Burned during the Imjin War, rebuilt around 1616. Extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. No gate symbol could be found on the original map, so it was positioned relative to the front of the model. The model is a two-story gate pavilion three bays wide.
- **Guards**: One gate captain (sumunjang) and two soldiers of the Eoyeongcheong (Royal Guards Command) were placed. This follows the record that the Eoyeongcheong kept watch at Honghwamun; the number of people is an estimate for display. ([History Net (Uri Yeoksa Net), palace-wall watch](https://contents.history.go.kr/front/nh/print.do?levelId=nh_030_0040_0050_0010_0040))
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Honghwamun](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0064444)

흥화문.body_en:
The main gate of Gyeongdeokgung (Gyeonghuigung from 1760). On the detail sheet the inscription 興化門 and a red-roofed gate symbol are drawn on the east wall, so it was placed there facing east.

- **Period of existence**: Founded under Gwanghaegun (1616 per the Korea Heritage portal, 1618 per Wikipedia). Moved to the south wall in 1915, to Bangmunsa temple in Jangchung-dong in 1932, and to the present Gyeonghuigung site in 1988. Extant, but not on its original site.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The model is a simplified single-story hip-roofed gate three bays wide.
- **Guards**: One gate captain and two soldiers were placed. Which military command guarded the gates of Gyeongdeokgung, and how many men, could not be confirmed, so this is an estimate for display.
- **Source**: [Korea Heritage portal, Heunghwamun of Gyeonghuigung](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?pageNo=1_1_2_0&ccbaCpno=2111100190000), [Korean Wikipedia, Heunghwamun](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%9D%A5%ED%99%94%EB%AC%B8)

경덕궁 (경희궁).body_en:
A secondary palace built by Gwanghaegun in the west of the capital. It is today's Gyeonghuigung, shown here under Gyeongdeokgung, its name at the map's reference date.

- **Period of existence**: Construction began in 1617. Renamed Gyeonghuigung in 1760 because "Gyeongdeok" sounded the same as the posthumous title of King Wonjong. Major fire in 1829, rebuilt in 1831. Most halls were dismantled in 1865 for materials to rebuild Gyeongbokgung, and after 1907 the Residency-General's middle school was built there, destroying the palace. Its main hall, Sungjeongjeon, was moved to the foot of Namsan in 1926 and is now Jeonggagwon at Dongguk University.
- **Around 1750**: It existed under the name Gyeongdeokgung.
- **Source**: [History Net, Gyeonghuigung 1617](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_r300210&code=kc_age_30), [Korea Heritage portal, Sungjeongjeon of Gyeonghuigung](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=2111100200000), [Korea Heritage Service, Royal Palaces and Tombs Center, Gyeonghuigung](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R110000000.do)

종묘.body_en:
The royal shrine housing the spirit tablets of the kings and queens of Joseon. The map shows the main hall (Jeongjeon) as a 15-bay gable-roofed building.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1395. Burned during the Imjin War, rebuilt in 1608. The main hall was enlarged to 15 bays in 1726 and to 19 bays in 1836. Extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The model's 15 bays match the bay count of 1726–1835.
- **Source**: [Korea Heritage Service, Royal Palaces and Tombs Center, history of Jongmyo](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R105010000.do)

어영청.body_en:
One of the Five Military Commands, responsible for guarding the king and defending the capital. Hyojong greatly expanded it for his planned northern expedition. Its headquarters, 505 bays in size, stood in Yeonhwabang east of the main gate of Jongmyo; the marker stone is in today's Inui-dong, Jongno-gu.

- **Period of existence**: Newly established in 1623 (Injo 1) as the king's bodyguard. Reorganized in 1652 (Hyojong 3). Merged with the Chongyungcheong and Geumwiyeong into the Jangeoyeong in 1881, became the Chongeoyeong in 1884, abolished in 1894.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The inscriptions east of Jongmyo on the original map are too low in resolution to be read as 御營廳. The Inui-dong location was adjusted to the south gate of Jongmyo on the original map, and it was placed between the Jongmyo wall and the main road, avoiding the north-south avenue.
- **Source**: [Korean Wikipedia, Eoyeongcheong](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%96%B4%EC%98%81%EC%B2%AD), [History Net, Eoyeongcheong](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/nh/view.do?levelId=nh_030_0040_0050_0010_0020), [History Net, Five Military Commands 1593–1884](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_o300820&code=kc_age_30)

사직단.title_en: Sajik Altar (Altar of Soil and Grain)
사직단.body_en:
The altar where sacrifices were offered to the god of soil (社) and the god of grain (稷). It is shown as a low marker box instead of a building.

- **Period of existence**: Laid out together with the construction of the capital in early Joseon. The exact year of construction and later changes are unconfirmed. Extant (Historic Site).
- **Around 1750**: It existed. Placed inside the walled enclosure on the original map.
- **Source**: [Korea Heritage Service, Royal Palaces and Tombs Center, Sajik Altar](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R311030000.do)

육상궁.body_en:
The shrine of Royal Noble Consort Suk of the Choe clan, the birth mother of Yeongjo. Yeongjo raised his mother's status and elevated it to a "gung" (palace shrine). It is the site of today's Chilgung (Seven Shrines).

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1725 (Yeongjo 1) as Sukbinmyo. Elevated to Yuksangmyo in 1744 and to Yuksanggung in 1753. Fire in 1882, rebuilt in 1883. Under Gojong and Sunjong the shrines Yeonhogung, Jeogyeonggung, Daebingung, Seonhuigung and Gyeongugung were moved here, and with the arrival of Deokangung in 1929 it became Chilgung. Extant.
- **Around 1750**: In 1750 it was Yuksangmyo. The Doseongdaejido labels it 毓祥宮, the name used from 1753, so it was placed at that inscription northwest of the Gyeongbokgung wall. Transferring the modern location of Chilgung onto the original map puts it about 100 m east of the inscription.
- **Source**: [Royal Palaces and Tombs Center, introduction and history of Chilgung](https://royal.khs.go.kr/ROYAL/contents/R107010000.do), [History Net, Yuksanggung 1725](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_r300763&code=kc_age_30), [Seoul City Wall Museum, Doseongdaejido](https://museum.seoul.go.kr/scwm/relic/RelicView.do?mcsjgbnc=PS01003026001&mcseqno1=014165&mcseqno2=00000&cdLanguage=KOR)

경모궁.body_en:
The shrine of Crown Prince Sado.

- **Period of existence**: Built in 1764 as Sueunmyo. Rebuilt after Jeongjo's accession in 1776 and renamed Gyeongmogung. Gyeongmowon in 1784, Gyeongmogung again in 1794. In 1899 Crown Prince Sado was posthumously honored as King Jangjo and his tablet moved to Jongmyo, ending its function as a shrine; Yeonghuijeon then took over the site. The site is now the area of Seoul National University Hospital.
- **Around 1750**: **It did not exist.** It was built after the map's reference date. It is not drawn on the original map, so it was placed at its modern location.
- **Source**: [History Net, Gyeongmogung 1764](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_r300150&code=kc_age_30), [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Gyeongmogung](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0002406)

문묘·성균관.title_en: Munmyo and Seonggyungwan (Confucian Shrine and National Academy)
문묘·성균관.body_en:
A complex combining the Munmyo, the shrine to Confucius (Daeseongjeon), and Seonggyungwan, the highest educational institution (Myeongnyundang).

- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. Burned during the Imjin War and rebuilt in the early 17th century. Detailed years unconfirmed. Extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. Placed within the buildings and walls on the original map.
- **Source**: [Korea Heritage digital service, Seoul Munmyo and Seonggyungwan](https://digital.khs.go.kr/heri/heriDetail.do?ctptNo=1121101410000&ctptUid=13898859667928200187)

한양도성의 문.title_en: Gates of the Seoul City Wall (Hanyang Doseong)
한양도성의 문.body_en:
The Seoul City Wall was first built in 1396 with four great gates and four small gates. The gates below were founded in early Joseon along with the wall itself; rebuilding dates of individual gate pavilions are given only where confirmed. ([Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do))

**About the models**: Each city-gate model consists of a dressed-stone base pierced by an arched passage (hongye), a parapet (yeojang) on top, and a gate pavilion with red columns, plastered walls and lattice windows. Sungnyemun and Heunginjimun have two-story pavilions; Donuimun and the four small gates have single-story pavilions, and the roofs are hip-and-gable (Sungnyemun closer to a hipped roof). A semicircular barbican (ongseong) stands in front of Heunginjimun. The barbican is known to have existed since the gate's founding in 1397, but the model is a conceptual one based on its appearance after the 1869 rebuilding, not a measured reconstruction. The gates were rotated to stand perpendicular to the local direction of the wall (only at Sungnyemun was the wall bent to fit the gate), and the passage direction was chosen from the approach-road axis read from the original map. Two spear-bearing soldiers stand on either side of the passage on the outer side of Sungnyemun, Heunginjimun and Donuimun (the outer side was defined as the side away from the center of the wall). Records say that under the 1751 "Suseong jeolmok" (Regulations for Defending the Wall) the three military commands divided responsibility for sections of the wall and that the royal guards stood duty at the city gates, but the number of men at each gate could not be confirmed, so this is an estimate for display. None were placed at Sukjeongmun, which was always kept closed, and at Gwanghwamun, which was in ruins, a single palace keeper (gunggam) was placed instead of soldiers. ([Cultural Heritage Administration, National Cultural Heritage portal, Heunginjimun, Seoul](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=1231100010000))

광화문.body_en:
The main gate of Gyeongbokgung. It is grouped with the city-gate models, but it is a palace gate, not a city-wall gate.

- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1395. Burned during the Imjin War, rebuilt in 1865–1868 during the reconstruction of Gyeongbokgung. After later relocation, destruction and restoration, it was restored to its original position in 2010.
- **Around 1750**: **There was no gate pavilion.** It lay in ruins together with Gyeongbokgung. The model marks the site with only a stone base with three arches; how much of the stone base survived at the time could not be confirmed.
- **Palace keeper**: A single palace keeper (gunggam) rests between the west and center arches on the south face of the stone base, then repeatedly walks through the center arch into the palace grounds, looks around, and comes back out. This follows research showing that a gunggam (palace keeper) was stationed at the ruined Gyeongbokgung in late Joseon to look after it. The keeper's position and attire (gat hat and dopo robe) are estimates for display. ([Yoo Jae-bin 2024, Korean Journal of Art History](https://www.kjah.org/journal/view.php?number=1929&viewtype=pubreader), [Korean Wikipedia, Gyeongbokgung](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B2%BD%EB%B3%B5%EA%B6%81))
- **Source**: [Wikidata, Gwanghwamun](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q485034)

숭례문 (남대문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Completed in 1398. Repaired many times; fire in 2008, restored in 2013. Extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed.
- **Source**: [Wikipedia, Sungnyemun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sungnyemun)

흥인지문 (동대문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in 1397; the barbican was built at the same time. The present building was newly rebuilt in 1869 under Gojong.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The model (two-story pavilion and barbican) is not a measured reconstruction of its appearance before the later rebuilding.
- **Source**: [Wikipedia, Heunginjimun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heunginjimun)

돈의문 (서대문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. After being relocated in early Joseon it was also called "Saemun" (New Gate). Demolished in 1915 and sold as building material. No longer extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed.
- **Source**: [Wikipedia, Donuimun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donuimun), [Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do)

창의문 (북소문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. Extant. The rebuilding date of the gate pavilion is unconfirmed.
- **Around 1750**: It existed.
- **Source**: [Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do)

숙정문 (북대문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. The gate pavilion was rebuilt during the wall restoration after 1968.
- **Around 1750**: The gate existed. Whether it had a pavilion at the time is unconfirmed.
- **Source**: [Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do)

혜화문 (동소문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. Gate pavilion removed in 1928; the arch and part of the wall removed in 1938. Later restored at a location other than the original site.
- **Around 1750**: It existed.
- **Source**: [Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do)

광희문 (남소문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. Gate pavilion collapsed in 1915. Later restored at a location other than the original site.
- **Around 1750**: It existed.
- **Source**: [Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do), [Korean Wikipedia, Gwanghuimun](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B4%91%ED%9D%AC%EB%AC%B8)

소의문 (서소문).body_en:
- **Period of existence**: Founded in early Joseon. Demolished in 1914. No longer extant.
- **Around 1750**: It existed.
- **Source**: [Seoul City Wall, history of the wall](https://seoulcitywall.seoul.go.kr/content/8.do)

육조거리 관청.title_en: Government Offices on Yukjo Street (the Six Ministries Street)
육조거리 관청.body_en:
The central government offices that lined both sides of the avenue in front of Gwanghwamun. The models draw on the circa-1863 layout and reconstruction images from the Seoul S-MAP Open Lab story map "Time Travel to Yukjo Street in the Joseon Period." The offices were established in early Joseon, the government structure changed greatly with the Gabo Reforms of 1894, and most of the buildings were demolished in the early 20th century. Demolition years for individual office buildings could not be confirmed.

- **Common source**: [Seoul S-MAP Open Lab, Time Travel to Yukjo Street in the Joseon Period](https://openlab.eseoul.go.kr/gallery/viewStoryMapContent.do?scid=NJDK-f3GQKD_3BA4XkZM5g)
- **Around 1750**: All of the institutions existed. However, the layout of the models follows circa-1863 material and does not establish the form of the buildings in 1750.
- **About the models**: The Yukjo Street offices and the other office compounds (`yukjo_compound`) are conceptual models following the typical layout of a Joseon government office. They consist of an outer three-gate entrance (oesammun, three bays with a raised center bay) in the middle of the front row of side halls, a central stone path in the courtyard, an inner three-gate entrance and wall on deeper lots, a main hall (jeongdang) on a stone platform with steps (7 bays for large offices, 5 bays for small ones, hip-and-gable roof), wing halls (ingnang, gable roofs) on either side of the courtyard, and an inner residence, storehouses and a well at the rear. On narrow lots the wing halls and rear buildings are reduced. The actual number of buildings, bay counts and layout of each office could not be confirmed. General features of office layouts were taken from the [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Gwana (government office)](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0004856).

| Office | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Uijeongbu (State Council) | The highest organ of government, led by the Chief, Left and Right State Councilors |
| Ijo (Ministry of Personnel) | Appointment of civil officials |
| Hojo (Ministry of Taxation) | Census, taxation and finance |
| Yejo (Ministry of Rites) | Rites, diplomacy, state examinations and education |
| Byeongjo (Ministry of War) | Appointment of military officials and military administration |
| Hyeongjo (Ministry of Justice) | Law, litigation and punishment |
| Gongjo (Ministry of Works) | Civil engineering, crafts and forestry |
| Hanseongbu (Capital Magistracy) | Administration and policing of the capital and its surroundings |
| Saheonbu (Office of the Inspector-General) | Inspection of officials and regulation of public morals |
| Jungchubu (Office of Ministers-without-Portfolio) | An office honoring senior officials without a current post |
| Hunguk Sinyeong (New Camp of the Military Training Command) | The new camp of the Hullyeon Dogam (Military Training Command) |

종루.body_en:
The pavilion that housed the bell announcing the hours when the city's traffic was opened and closed. It stood at the Unjongga crossroads, the site of today's Bosingak.

- **Period of existence**: In 1398 a bell was first hung at the bell pavilion west of Cheongungyo bridge. In 1413 it was moved to today's Jongno crossroads. In 1440 it was rebuilt at a size of 5 bays east-west by 4 bays north-south, with the bell hung on the upper floor. Burned during the Imjin War. Rebuilt in 1619 under Gwanghaegun, this time as a **single-story bell house**. The "Bosingak" plaque was hung in 1895. The present building was rebuilt as a two-story structure in 1979.
- **Bell**: A bell cast in 1468 was hung in this pavilion after the Imjin War. Height 3.18 m, mouth diameter 2.28 m. It is now in the National Museum of Korea.
- **Around 1750**: The bell hung in the single-story bell house built in 1619. The map model is also a single-story bell house, and its bay count follows the recorded 5 × 4 bays of 1440.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Bosingak site](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0023446), [Korean Wikipedia, Bosingak](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%B3%B4%EC%8B%A0%EA%B0%81), [Korea Heritage portal, old Bosingak bronze bell](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=1121100020000)

운종가 시전 행랑.title_en: Sijeon Arcades (Licensed Shop Rows) of Unjongga
운종가 시전 행랑.body_en:
Rows of shops built by the state and leased to merchants. A shop-row tax was collected per bay, and the sijeon (licensed shops) bearing the heaviest state-service obligations were grouped as the Yugujeon (the Six Licensed Shops).

- **Period of existence**: From 1412 (Taejong 12), three rounds of construction built 2,027 bays of arcades. The arcades ran from Hyejeonggyo bridge to the entrance of Changdeokgung. The sijeon system continued into late Joseon. When the system ended and when the arcade buildings disappeared were not confirmed in this document.
- **Around 1750**: They existed. Individual arcade buildings are not drawn on the original map, so they were lined up for display along the roads read from it.
- **Sijeon on signboards**: Seonjeon (Chinese silk, around Gwangtonggyo bridge), Myeonpojeon (cotton cloth, around Gwangtonggyo and the bell pavilion), Myeonjujeon (Korean silk, around the bell pavilion), Naeeomuljeon (dried fish, around the bell pavilion), Jeopojeon (ramie, near Jongno 3-ga). The shops given signboards and their shapes are for display.
- **Source**: [History Net, sijeon commerce in the new capital in early Joseon](https://contents.history.go.kr/front/km/view.do?levelId=km_003_0040_0020_0010), [History Net, wholesale houses and sijeon arcades](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/km/view.do?levelId=km_003_0040_0040_0050_0010), [History Net, Yugujeon](https://contents.history.go.kr/front/km/view.do?levelId=km_003_0040_0030_0010), [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, sijeon](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0032450)

Clicking an arcade shows the description of the sijeon for that section (Seonjeon, Myeonpojeon, Myeonjujeon, Naeeomuljeon, Jeopojeon). All five belonged to the Yugujeon. The box marker that represented Unjongga as a whole was removed in v0.1.13.

원각사지 십층석탑.title_en: Ten-Story Stone Pagoda at the Wongaksa Temple Site
원각사지 십층석탑.body_en:
The marble ten-story pagoda of Wongaksa, the temple founded by Sejo. The temple disappeared but the pagoda remained, and in late Joseon it was called the White Pagoda (Baektap). It is the site of today's Tapgol Park.

- **Period of existence**: Wongaksa founded in 1465, pagoda erected in 1467. The temple was abolished in 1504 under Yeonsangun. Around the time of the Imjin War the top three stories fell and were set beside the pagoda; they were put back in 1947. Extant (National Treasure).
- **Around 1750**: Only seven stories stood, with the top three set beside it. The model shows it that way. Both the original Doseongdaejido and the detail sheets are torn in this area, so the modern location was adjusted to the Jangtonggyo and Supyogyo bridges drawn on the original map and placed north of the stretch between the two bridges, west of Supyogyo.
- **Source**: [Korea Heritage portal, Ten-Story Stone Pagoda at Wongaksa Temple Site, Seoul](https://www.heritage.go.kr/heri/cul/culSelectDetail.do?ccbaCpno=1111100020000), [History Net, Ten-Story Stone Pagoda at Wongaksa Temple Site 1467](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_r300756&code=kc_age_30), [Korean Wikipedia, Ten-Story Stone Pagoda at Wongaksa Temple Site, Seoul](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%84%9C%EC%9A%B8_%EC%9B%90%EA%B0%81%EC%82%AC%EC%A7%80_%EC%8B%AD%EC%B8%B5%EC%84%9D%ED%83%91)

의금부.body_en:
The office that, by royal command, handled serious offenders such as those accused of treason. It stood northwest of the Jongno crossroads, north of Pimatgil.

- **Period of existence**: Established in early Joseon. Reorganized around the Gabo Reforms of 1894. Detailed years unconfirmed.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The inscription 義禁府 was confirmed on the Doseongdaejido detail sheet and it was placed clear of the roads.
- **Source**: [Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Uigeumbu](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0043266)

좌포도청·우포도청.body_en:
Police offices that suppressed thieves and crime inside and outside the capital. The Left Podocheong covered the eastern part of the city, the Right Podocheong the western part.

- **Location**: The Left Podocheong is said to have been in the area of the Dansungsa theater in Myo-dong, Jongno-gu, and the Right Podocheong in the area of 89 Jongno 1-ga.
- **Period of existence**: Established in early Joseon. Replaced by the Gyeongmucheong (Police Agency) in the Gabo Reforms of 1894. Detailed years unconfirmed.
- **Around 1750**: They existed. The Left Podocheong was placed at the inscription 左捕廳 on the Doseongdaejido detail sheet. No symbol was found for the Right Podocheong, so it was placed at a display position north of Unjongga.
- **Source**: [History Net, Podocheong](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/kc/view.do?levelId=kc_o301320&code=kc_age_30)

혜민서.body_en:
The medical office that treated the illnesses of commoners, distributed medicine and trained female physicians (uinyeo). The site is at 65 Euljiro 3-ga, Jung-gu, near Euljiro 3-ga Station.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392 as Hyemingoguk, renamed Hyeminguk in 1414 and Hyeminseo in 1466 (Sejo 12). Abolished in 1882.
- **Around 1750**: It existed. The Doseongdaejido detail sheet has the inscription 惠民署 in a yellow box, so it was placed there. The original map is heavily distorted in this area, so transferring the modern location directly would put it far east of the Supyogyo bridge on the original map.
- **Source**: [Korean Wikipedia, Hyeminseo](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%98%9C%EB%AF%BC%EC%84%9C), [History Net, Hyeminseo](https://contents.history.go.kr/mobile/nh/view.do?levelId=nh_025_0040_0010_0020_0050), [History Net, textbook glossary, Hyeminseo](https://contents.history.go.kr/front/tg/view.do?levelId=tg_003_0730)

훈련원.body_en:
A senior third-rank office that administered the military examinations and was responsible for martial arts training and instruction in military tactics. South of its main building it had a wide field used for archery and examinations. The site is the area of today's Hullyeonwon Park on Euljiro, Jung-gu.

- **Period of existence**: Established in 1392 as Hullyeongwan. Moved to this site under Taejong, when an archery hall was built south of the main building. Renamed Hullyeonwon in 1466. The date of abolition was not confirmed in this document.
